docs.abstract: Still asking: Does force-feeding detainees amount to torture?
docs.snippet: Still asking: Does force-feeding detainees amount to torture?
docs.lead_paragraph: Jihad Ahmed Mujstafa Diyab is a Syrian man who has been a detainee at the prison in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 2002. In 2009, the Guantánamo Review Task Force ruled that he was not a threat to national security and could be released. Yet here we are five years later, and Diyab is still imprisoned at Guantánamo, having never been tried, or even accused of a crime, and with no idea when — or if — he’ll ever get out. Last year, to protest their continued confinement, he and many other detainees began a hunger strike. Most of the detainees have since given up their hunger strikes. Diyab, however, has never completely stopped his.

headline.main: The Guantánamo Tapes

docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: The French mourn their dead in 1914.
docs.lead_paragraph: All Souls’ Day, when French custom decrees one shall make a pilgrimage to the tombs of the dead, is always an impressive occasion in Paris, but yesterday was especially so, owing to the bereavements of the war, and the great outpouring of the public to the cemeteries at Pantin, Ivry and Bagneux, where soldiers fallen in the conflict have been buried. It was a throng typically Parisian, typically proletariat, which filed through the massive stone gates of the cemetery at Bagneux to the section where most of the soldiers who have died in the great military hospital of Val-de-Grâce lie buried. Perhaps half of the women were hatless. Many carried children in their arms. By half-past two o’clock in the afternoon the street in front of the cemetery was an unbroken phalanx moving toward the gates. At half-past four, when the autumn sun was disappearing behind the trees, the stream was still coming from Paris. — The New York Herald, European Edition, Nov. 3, 1914

headline.main: 1914: Parisians Flock to Cemeteries on All Souls’ Day to Honor Dead Soldiers

docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: American ships rush to sail before a neutrality bill goes into effect, prohibiting travel to states designated as belligerent.
docs.lead_paragraph: NEW YORK — United States liners and freighters scheduled to sail for belligerent ports tonight [Nov. 2 ] speeded preparations to get away within the next day or two before the Administration’s neutrality bill, passed by the House of Representatives today, would become effective. The United States liner Washington, scheduled to sail for Europe next Wednesday, will leave New York tomorrow morning, and the President Roosevelt is sailing tomorrow noon instead of Saturday. The American Farmer will make a special trip without passengers, sailing today or tomorrow. Under the terms of the existing neutrality legislation American vessels are permitted to carry merchandise of a non-military nature to belligerent ports, but when the new law goes into effect, all American ships will be forbidden to enter the waters of states designated as belligerents by the President. Although ships of the United States merchant marine may not call at French, British or German ports in the actual war zone, they may carry cargo and passengers to ports belonging to the belligerents definitely outside the zone of combat, such as Australia, New Zealand, India, Indo-China and the West Indies. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, Nov. 3, 1939

headline.main: 1939: American Ships Hasten to Sail Before New Bill Takes Effect

docs.abstract: John Spinello, inventor of what became the board game Operation in 1965, is able to afford a $25,000 dental procedure because of a crowdfunding campaign.
docs.snippet: John Spinello, inventor of what became the board game Operation in 1965, is able to afford a $25,000 dental procedure because of a crowdfunding campaign.
docs.lead_paragraph: Cavity Sam of the classic board game Operation recently got a makeover, and the man who helped create him will, too. John Spinello, above, inventor of what became Operation in 1965, is able to afford a $25,000 dental procedure because of a crowdfunding campaign begun by his fellow game inventors Tim Walsh and Peggy Brown. The campaign, which began Oct. 22 at crowdrise.com, raised over $31,000 by early Sunday. The experience, Mr. Spinello said by phone from Bloomington, Ill., has been “mind boggling.” “It’s really rewarding to have people calling me right now from all over the world,” he said. “You can’t put a price tag on it.” Mr. Spinello, 77, invented the buzzer game while studying industrial design at the University of Illinois. He sold his idea to a toy invention firm for $500, and it was then licensed to Milton Bradley. Through the years there have been various riffs on the character, including Homer Simpson, SpongeBob SquarePants and a version with 21st-century ailments like headphone headache and gamer’s thumb. Though Mr. Spinello still owns the patent for the game, he said he receives no royalties. In recent years, the recession hurt his trucking warehouse company, and he and his wife have filed for bankruptcy. In addition to the donations at Crowdrise, money has also been raised through the sale of signed copies of the game and $3 “Dear John” thank-you letters at iloveoperation.com. Hasbro, which owns Milton Bradley, has pitched in by agreeing to buy the original prototype from Mr. Spinello. Calls requesting comment from Hasbro were not returned. Mr. Spinello said he hoped any leftover money would go to saving his home. But, he added, he would be grateful for “a decent smile and the ability to chew.”

docs.abstract: The Virginia estate of President James Madison may soon look more like the home he knew, through a $10 million gift from the businessman and philanthropist David Rubenstein.
docs.snippet: The Virginia estate of President James Madison may soon look more like the home he knew, through a $10 million gift from the businessman and philanthropist David Rubenstein.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Virginia estate of President James Madison may soon look more like the home he knew, complete with 19th-century furnishings and slave quarters, through a $10 million gift from the businessman and philanthropist David Rubenstein. The Montpelier Foundation announced on Saturday that the money would be used to further restore the mansion to its original 1817 appearance and provide more context about the lives of Madison’s slaves. Part of the gift, $3.5 million, will support reconstruction of the mansion’s south yard, where the family’s domestic servants lived and worked. The plans include three slave quarters, two smokehouses and a detached kitchen. The rest of the money will go toward restoring, researching and refurnishing the home, including purchasing items authentic to the time period or the home; much of what was there has been dispersed over the years through family members or sales. Dolley Madison sold the property in 1844 after her husband’s death, and Montpelier had various owners until it was purchased in 1901 by William duPont. In 1984, it was bestowed to the National Trust for Historic Preservation by Marion duPont Scott, following her death in 1983. This is Mr. Rubenstein’s third major recent gift to presidential estates in Virginia.

headline.main: $10 Million Gift for Madison Estate

docs.abstract: To define other species as “nonpolitical” excludes them from consideration as beings with interests of their own. What’s wrong with that?
docs.snippet: To define other species as “nonpolitical” excludes them from consideration as beings with interests of their own. What’s wrong with that?
docs.lead_paragraph: Homo sapiens has long sought to set itself apart from animals — that is, apart from every other living species. One of the most enduring attempts to define humanity in a way that distances us from the rest of animal life was Aristotle’s description of the human being as a “political animal.” By this he meant that human beings are the only species that live in the “polis” or city-state, though the term has often been understood to include villages, communes, and other organized social units. Implicit in this definition is the idea that all other animals are not political, that they live altogether outside of internally governed social units.

headline.main: We Are Not the Only Political Animals

docs.lead_paragraph: Few mammals are as unloved as the wolf. Not that the feeling is universal. Some North American Indian tribes traditionally honored the predator as a worthy fellow hunter. (CMT) WINTER’S BONE (2010) Jennifer Lawrence, above, received her first Oscar nomination for her role as Ree Dolly, a teenager living in the Ozarks of southwestern Missouri who goes in search of her meth-cooking father after he puts up the family home to cover his bail and disappears. But her efforts to find him place her in a terrible dilemma: either betray the code of silence that keeps her clan proudly on the wrong side of the law or face destitution. The harshness in Debra Granik’s “regional-realist morality tale,” based on the novel by Daniel Woodrell, “is not there to illuminate a sociological condition,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times. “Something more primal, almost Greek in its archaic power, is at stake in ‘Winter’s Bone,’ and its visual and emotional starkness do not feel like simple badges of authenticity.”

The people lining the route manifested much enthusiasm, particularly the Germans. It is estimated that nearly two hundred thousand people were in the streets to see their Majesties pass. The Sultan and his Ministers have spared no trouble or expense to combine a gorgeous ceremonial with the comfort of the Emperor and Empress, and these in turn have evinced an almost juvenile pleasure in what they have seen, whilst the attitude of the general public has been all that could be desired. The New York Philharmonic gave the work its premiere in 1893, but when Dvorak returned to Prague in 1895, he took the manuscript of the symphony with him. docs.lead_paragraph: For 14 years, the famed photographer Bruce Weber has published an annual anthology of essays, poetry and images that celebrates, with his trademark patriotism, everything from canines to cops to mountain climbers. The book’s latest edition, “Affairs of the Heart,” includes stories about the late novelist and C.I.A. agent Peter Matthiessen as well as one on a boarding school for equestrians, and features contributions by art-world heavyweights like Francesco Clemente. Most notable, however, is a piece on Kris Ruhs, the New York City-born sculptor responsible for the amazing three-story chandelier at the Azzedine Alaïa store in Paris and the silver jewelry sold by Carla Sozzani (his companion and frequent collaborator) at her Milan boutique-bookstore-gallery-cafe 10 Corso Como. Weber had previously encountered Ruhs’s workspace when he shot the actress Marion Cotillard in the sculptor’s Paris studio four years ago. “The day just flew by,” Weber recalls, “because we were so enchanted by the things that Kris had made.”

headline.main: When Bruce Met Ruhs

docs.abstract: Where the immigration issue fits into the weakening of the president.
docs.snippet: Where the immigration issue fits into the weakening of the president.
docs.lead_paragraph: My Sunday column considered various possible and partial explanations for President Obama’s long year of low approval ratings, which seem likely to help cost his party control of the Senate tomorrow. The big four I considered were structural forces (the idea that polarization and gridlock alone suffice to send most second-term presidents regressing to the low 40s), the essential mediocrity of our “recovered” economy, the continued unpopularity of Obamacare, and foreign policy (where the president’s approval ratings have fallen hard) as a kind of synecdoche for larger doubts about the administration’s basic competence. Obviously there are many more factors one could consider, but since I write about the issue frequently I thought I should explain why I didn’t include immigration, another area where the president’s approval numbers have plummeted as his administration has stumbled in various ways over the last year.

headline.main: Immigration and Obama’s Swoon

docs.snippet: The Sanrio character, who turns 40 this year, was the star of a suite of events that began on Wednesday at MOCA’s Geffen Contemporary. The photographer Jacqueline DiMilia captured the style scene in and around the show.
docs.lead_paragraph: Red carpets and celebrities are a dime a dozen in L.A., but this past weekend the city feted an icon unlike any other. Hello Kitty, who turns 40 this year, was the star of a suite of events that began on Wednesday with the opening of the first annual Hello Kitty Convention. The carnival-meets-trade fair drew more than 26,000 Sanrio disciples dressed to the nines, plus several stars from the Nickelodeon set and the superfan Katy Perry, to MOCA’s Geffen Contemporary in Little Tokyo. Highlights included musical performances, scholarly panels on licensing and globalization, live appearances and, last but not least, shopping, while some of the strangest sights included watching Kitty christen the Friendship Village pop-up shop as she bought a cartload of merchandise featuring herself, and the tattoo parlor that offered attendees a spectrum of free, permanent body art (Perry partook). The photographer Jacqueline DiMilia captured the style scene in and around the show; for those craving a closer look, the companion exhibition at the Japanese American National Museum next door, “Hello! Exploring the Supercute World of Hello Kitty,” is on view through April 26 of next year.

headline.main: Scenes From the Hello Kitty Convention in Los Angeles
headline.print_headline: Happenings: The Cat’s Meow

docs.lead_paragraph: The African Union on Monday gave Burkina Faso’s military leaders two weeks to return power to a civilian-led government or face severe sanctions. The warning by the Peace and Security Council of the 54-nation organization, posted on its Twitter account after an emergency meeting in Ethiopia, came as the country’s interim president, Lt. Col. Isaac Zida, sought to assure diplomats and residents that the military takeover of the government on Friday was only temporary. The armed forces seized control after the longtime president, Blaise Compaoré, fled amid mass protests over his efforts to engineer a vote that would have allowed him to stay in office indefinitely. The United States government, which is legally obliged to suspend aid to countries where power is usurped by the military, did not immediately take a position on whether the events in Burkina Faso had amounted to a coup. “We’re still gathering facts,” said Jen Psaki, a State Department spokeswoman. “We’re not going to make a policy or legal determination at this point in time.”

headline.main: Burkina Faso: A Regional Warning

docs.lead_paragraph: People who pay for college with federal student loans can avoid default when they fall on hard times by making lower payments — or no payments at all — until they recover financially. Borrowers who take out private student loans from banks and other institutions typically have no such option. When they lose their jobs or suffer other financial setbacks, they have little choice but to default, which, in turn, damages their credit histories and ability to borrow for other purposes or even to find a job.

(HBO Signature) ADMISSION (2013) Tina Fey portrays Portia Nathan, a Princeton admissions officer who seems to take a special kind of glee in controlling the fate of applicants aspiring to the university. She also has a goal of her own: to succeed the retiring dean of admissions (Wallace Shawn) and beat out her office rival (Gloria Reuben) while reclaiming Princeton’s place at the top of the U.S. News & World Report rankings. But just as her smug English-professor boyfriend (Michael Sheen) dumps her for an aggressive Virginia Woolf scholar (Sonya Walger), a fellow Dartmouth alum (Paul Rudd) comes along with an unusual student (Nat Wolff) he wants Portia to consider. “How could anyone make light of the brutal, capricious system by which our young people are judged and sorted?” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times about this comedy from Paul Weitz, adapted from the novel by Jean Hanff Korelitz. “I must confess that I don’t know whether to be relieved or disappointed that ‘Admission,’ which had the potential to be a sharp, satirical jab at the soft belly of middle-class anxiety, chose instead to be a warm and wacky fable of wish fulfillment.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Observing my patient through the chicken wire, I saw that the front half of his scalp was shaved — and the long gray hairs behind that equator were gathered in a kudumi, or knot. But his discomfort was real. In my recollection, he sits cross-legged on his mat in that locked room, groaning, restless, his trunk swaying, his features anxious, grimacing as if he’d tasted something bitter.

Lately several cases of severe and stubborn sickness have been attributed to some unknown witch, and for that reason pillows and feather beds were opened and carefully examined. The bunches formed inside are called crowns, wreaths, chickens or any imaginable thing. A case a few days ago of this description happened. A hot fire was made, and the crowns and such put in the fire, but would not burn; even the feathers would not be scorched; but while wondering about it, they had suddenly disappeared. — The New York Herald, European Edition, Nov. 05, 1889

docs.abstract: The midterms and the expectations game.
docs.snippet: The midterms and the expectations game.
docs.lead_paragraph: You won’t get formal midterm predictions from me today — that’s why we have Mr. Silver’s difference engine and Mr. Leonhardt’s Skynet, surely — but I do have a couple of thoughts on the debate over what the midterm results mean for the Republican Party’s political position overall. Over the weekend, as the Republican advantage seemed to solidify, a number of writers made the point that the G.O.P. could probably win the Senate without making the kind of inroads that would bode well for their chances of winning the White House (or even keeping the Senate) two years hence. This year’s midterm map is unusually unrepresentative of the country as a whole, the Washington Post’s Patrick Egan noted, and so tonight’s outcomes don’t tell us that much about the future; the G.O.P. is winning more on second-term disillusionment than on any positive vision or agenda, two the party’s pollsters argued in the same newspaper, and isn’t showing any signs of expanding the electoral map into blue territory. The upshot (if you will) of these patterns, my colleague Nate Cohn suggested, is that Republicans are poised to retake the Senate without winning over “many voters who supported President Obama in 2012″ — an outcome that would indicate they’ve “made little progress in attracting voters they would need to take back the White House.”

headline.main: For Republicans, What Counts as Victory?

docs.abstract: The answer: It depends. That said, here are some things to consider if you’re visiting Amsterdam, Madrid, Florence or Paris.
docs.snippet: The answer: It depends. That said, here are some things to consider if you’re visiting Amsterdam, Madrid, Florence or Paris.
docs.lead_paragraph: Visit the tourism office in any major city in Europe and you’ll most likely find an offer to purchase a museum pass – a card that gives the holder entry to multiple local museums. Some passes include additional perks – priority entrance, discounts at monuments, free use of public transportation – but the high prices have always left me skeptical: These passes are marketed to tourists as a way to save money, but how many museums do you need to visit before you’ve recouped the cost of the pass? And were all of those museums already on your itinerary? To determine if the passes really are bargains, I examined the offers in four museum-dense European cities popular with travelers: Amsterdam, Madrid, Florence and Paris. So what’s the verdict on these supposed money-savers? It depends on the city – and on the traveler’s interests, allotted time and stamina.

headline.main: Are European Museum Passes Worth the Money?

docs.lead_paragraph: Protests broke out in Indian-administered Kashmir on Tuesday, a day after Indian soldiers fatally shot two people in a car that did not stop at a checkpoint. They and two others who were wounded were all civilians. Crowds of protesters in the main city, Srinagar, chanted anti-Indian slogans and threw stones at officials, and separatist organizations called for a strike on Wednesday. The Indian soldiers were on high alert after a huge  explosion on Sunday on the Pakistan side of the border that killed 50 people. Omar Abdullah, the chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir State, described the deaths as “avoidable” and discussed the matter with India’s defense minister, Arun Jaitley.

headline.main: Kashmir Protests Follow Shootings

docs.snippet: As their military struggles to combat the Islamist terrorist group, everyday Nigerians have formed citizen battalions to defend their towns. But have they gone too far?
docs.lead_paragraph: Long before the Islamist militant group Boko Haram kidnapped nearly 300 schoolgirls from Chibok in April, Abba Aji Kalli watched his country descend into madness. Kalli lives in Maiduguri, a city of more than one million and the capital of Borno State, just 80 miles from Chibok, in Nigeria’s impoverished northeast. For months before the girls were taken, refugees flooded into Maiduguri, fleeing almost-daily Boko Haram raids on nearby villages. The militants arrived on motorcycles and Toyota Hilux trucks, sometimes in the middle of the night, sometimes in broad daylight, destroying homes and businesses and killing villagers. By May, a month after the kidnappings, the rebels were coming closer, striking surrounding villages and towns. Maiduguri could only be next.

headline.main: Inside the Vigilante Fight Against Boko Haram

docs.lead_paragraph: The 25th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall would hardly seem the occasion for an entrancing picture book, but the British author-illustrator Tom Clohosy Cole’s “Wall” is just that. The narrator is a little boy stuck in East Berlin with his mother and sister, while his father has ended up in the West. Out of this wrenching scenario Cole has fashioned a tight little narrative that has all the ambient foreboding of a fairy tale, the sense of children at the mercy of enormous, irrational, half-understood forces. But with a morose, shadowy palette of midnight blues and browns and a flat, elongated look that calls to mind Cold War poster art, it’s clear that the evil lurking is a distinctly modern one: jackboots and rifles, not malevolent spells, but what’s the difference to a child whose parent has been taken away?

headline.main: Digging to Freedom

docs.lead_paragraph: The good news is that you still can’t flush the toilet paper in Tulum. The plumbing, like the balmy weather and a tenacious iguana population, is deeply rooted in the identity of this town an hour and a half south of Cancún. But even a quasi-functional plumbing infrastructure can’t dissuade tourists. Which leads me to the less good news. If you haven’t been to Tulum in the last few years, a heads-up: It’s a whole lot bigger than you remember. Today’s Tulum has three things many never thought possible: traffic, crowds and restaurants with waiting lists. But don’t despair. In fact, the town (it’s not a village anymore) is more exciting than ever. The beach is still stunning. The ruins are still there. The food is spicy and authentic. And for those willing, there are secret gems a long, dusty way from the beaten path.

docs.lead_paragraph: LOU HARRISON: ‘La Koro Sutro’ and Suite for Violin with American GamelanBoston Modern Orchestra Project, Gil Rose, conductor; Gabriela Diaz, violinist; Providence Singers(BMOP/sound 1037)The American maverick composer Lou Harrison (1917-2003), like his colleague John Cage, was a pioneering explorer of Asian music. He was also an innovative builder of instruments. He and his lifelong partner, Bill Colvig, built sets of tuned percussion instruments that they called the American gamelan. This rewarding new recording offers a captivating performance of a Harrison masterpiece for this instrument, the Suite for Violin with American Gamelan, with the fine violinist Gabriela Diaz as soloist. The other enticement here is Harrison’s beguiling, delicate, melodically haunting “La Koro Sutro,” a setting of an Esperanto adaptation of the traditional Buddhist text the Heart Sutra, with the Providence Singers. docs.snippet: Fabiola Gianotti, who led one of the two teams of physicists that discovered the Higgs boson, the so-called God particle that imbues other particles with mass, has been named the next director general of CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear...
docs.lead_paragraph: Fabiola Gianotti, who led one of the two teams of physicists that discovered the Higgs boson, the so-called God particle that imbues other particles with mass, has been named the next director-general of CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. Dr. Gianotti, 52, will take over for a five-year run at the end of 2015, when the current director, Rolf-Dieter Heuer, steps down. She will be the first woman to direct the laboratory — which is outside Geneva and is home to the world’s most expensive science experiment, the Large Hadron Collider — where the Higgs boson was finally produced and detected in 2012, capping a half-century quest. The machine, which has been down for repairs for the past two years, is to fire up its proton beams again next March with higher energies in the hunt for better understanding of the new boson and of other mysteries, like the nature of dark matter.

headline.main: Switzerland: Next Director Is Named for CERN Nuclear Laboratory

docs.lead_paragraph: The United Nations war crimes tribunal in The Hague has proposed a temporary release for Vojislav Seselj, a Serbian nationalist leader with cancer, whose health has seriously deteriorated during his long-running trial. In a decision published on Wednesday, the judge in charge of his case suggested that “to avoid the worst-case scenario” Mr. Seselj should return to Serbia for treatment. Mr. Seselj, a firebrand politician, has been charged with inciting others to commit war crimes in Bosnia and Croatia in the 1990s by creating a militia and sending its members off with incendiary speeches. He has also been convicted of contempt of court. Mr. Seselj surrendered to the tribunal in 2003, and his enduring presence during his much-delayed trial has become an embarrassment for the Yugoslavia tribunal. He has often harangued judges and has taken pride in provoking prosecutors.

headline.main: The Hague: Serbian Nationalist Leader With Cancer May Be Freed Temporarily

docs.snippet: Eugene Kaspersky’s global computer security company, Kaspersky Lab, is a major sponsor of the Ferrari Formula One team.
docs.lead_paragraph: Eugene Kaspersky, 49, is co-founder, chairman and chief executive of Kaspersky Lab, one of the world’s leading providers of antivirus technology for computers. Kaspersky, who was born in Novorossiysk, Russia, graduated in 1987 from the Russian Institute of Cryptography, Telecommunications and Computer Science with a degree in computer technology and mathematical engineering. In 1989, while working for the Soviet military as a cryptographer, he discovered a virus in his computer and began to study and treat it. He did the same for another colleague who had found a virus in his computer. By 1991, Kaspersky had moved to a private company, where he and his colleagues developed a program called AntiViral Toolkit Pro. That was the prototype for what became the Kaspersky Anti-Virus, now sold by Kaspersky Lab, the company that he founded in 1997. Based in Moscow, the company now has 30 regional offices and works in nearly 200 countries. The company became a sponsor in Formula One with the Ferrari team in 2010 and has expanded into one of the team’s major sponsors and technical partners. Kaspersky’s software is used in the Ferrari computer system and he plans additional projects within the series. Kaspersky is a racing fan and he occasionally drives sports cars on racetracks for fun. As part of an occasional series focusing on famous and unusual Formula One fans, Kaspersky spoke recently with Brad Spurgeon of the International New York Times.

docs.lead_paragraph: There are 1.27 million lawyers in the United States, one for about every 300 Americans — about 400,000 more of them than there are doctors. Their work is rarely glamorous, and especially for those just starting out in the profession, it can be grinding and repetitive. Jason Luckasevic, hired out of law school in 2000 by a firm in Pittsburgh, passed the bar exam on his first try and was quickly sworn in to practice. The ceremony, such as it was, took place on a Thursday in a clerk’s office, rather than in a courtroom in front of family and friends, because his bosses needed him to get started. The following Monday morning, he drove to Johnstown, about 90 minutes away, where he spent the day taking depositions from former employees of an enormous steel plant that had exposed them to asbestos. Late that afternoon, he climbed back into his Honda Civic and headed home. He repeated this routine for the next six months, five days a week, racking up some 400 depositions and about 20,000 miles on the road.

headline.main: How One Lawyer’s Crusade Could Change Football Forever

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The man who discovered the Cullinan Diamond died in 1939.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The man who discovered the Cullinan Diamond died in 1939.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — Sir Thomas Cullinan, whose name the famous Cullinan diamond bears, has died at his home in Johannesburg, South Africa, at the age of seventy-nine. Founder and director of the first organized diamond mining company during his youth, he became known throughout the world in 1905 with the discovery of the ‘‘Cullinan’’ diamond. With its weight of 3,025.75 carats, it was by far the largest diamond ever found. The government of the Transvaal presented the great diamond to King Edward VII of Great Britain. Amsterdam cutters fashioned nine large gems and many smaller ones from it. The two most beautiful today belong to the British royal treasure, one being on the crown of King George VI and the other in his sceptre. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, Nov. 7, 1939

headline.main: 1939: Sir Thomas Cullinan Dies

docs.lead_paragraph: The artist might be present, and then again, she might not. For her last, spectacularly popular outing in New York, “The Artist Is Present” (2010), the performance diva Marina Abramovic sat in the Museum of Modern Art’s atrium and silently exchanged gazes with other people, one person at a time, for hours and days on end. “Generator,” a participatory exercise in sensory deprivation at the Sean Kelly Gallery, doesn’t depend on Ms. Abramovic’s charismatic personal presence. docs.abstract: Five picture books directly address young readers with unconventional storytelling.
docs.snippet: Five picture books directly address young readers with unconventional storytelling.
docs.lead_paragraph: Have your kids gone meta? Do they call their neighborhood jungle gym a “play structure”? Do they mix and match their dress-up garb — a tiara here, firefighter’s boots there — with a sense of mischief that might, unnervingly, be termed “ironic”? Have they spotted the clown at the neighbor’s birthday party removing his wig and slinking out the side door? They’re probably not ready for the labyrinthine tricksterism of David Foster Wallace or Spike Jonze. But on the evidence of a recent spate of highly self-conscious picture books, it would seem that the suspended-disbelief state of early childhood is adapting to the wink-wink, nudge-nudge sensibility of our moment. It’s not surprising. There has long been a strain of subversion in picture books — think of Maurice Sendak and Tomi Ungerer, among others — alongside the dominant anodyne snuggliness of the form. Now, sophisticated cheekiness appears to have gone mainstream. These five specimens of reinvention deftly pop the bubbles of their own illusory worlds, drawing attention to the artifices of their norms and aiming to teach children to become not just book lovers but pint-size “consumers of text.” The best of these books, luckily, manage to find fresh magic in demystification, and to delight kids while spinning the heads of their grown-up companions.

headline.main: B. J. Novak’s ‘Book With No Pictures’ and More

docs.lead_paragraph: Have the Walt Disney and Pixar animation studios become Walt Pixar, or maybe Wixar or Dixar? It’s getting hard to tell these once-distinct siblings apart. Disney’s latest animated feature, “Big Hero 6,” is a bright, visually sumptuous 3-D computer-animated feature that gives you a bit of an emotional workout. It doesn’t have some of the familiar Disney markers: There are no eardrum-busting anthems or warbling critters, and it isn’t a fairy tale, exactly, mostly because it’s about a boy. It’s a Disney superhero movie with a story from a Marvel comic book, if one rendered with the wit and texture often associated with Pixar, which I guess makes it a Walt Pixar Marvel.

docs.abstract: In the early 1900s, an 18-block area of New Orleans was a battleground between moral reformers and purveyors of vice.
docs.snippet: In the early 1900s, an 18-block area of New Orleans was a battleground between moral reformers and purveyors of vice.
docs.lead_paragraph: When Tom Anderson’s saloon opened in 1901, at the entrance to the recently designated sin district known as Storyville on the edge of New Orleans’s French Quarter, people from all over town came to marvel at its opulence. Its cherrywood bar stretched half a block and was lit by a hundred electric lights. With Anderson’s encouragement, high-class brothels were soon flourishing down Basin Street. Josie Arlington, his business partner, had a four-story Victorian mansion with a domed cupola, mirrored parlor and Oriental statues. The exotic, mixed-race Lulu White built a brick palace that specialized in interracial sex and featured the jazz pioneer Jelly Roll Morton at the piano. Another octoroon (the appellation given to people considered to be one-eighth black), Willie V. Piazza, passed herself off as a countess and sported both a monocle and a diamond choker. Anderson, whose civic spirit earned him the title “the Mayor of Storyville,” published a Blue Book that contained photos and descriptions of the area’s better prostitutes, annotated with symbols (“w” for white, “c” for colored, “J” for Jewish and “oct.” for octoroon). It was all a vivid expression of the city’s tolerance and diversity.

headline.main: ‘Empire of Sin,’ by Gary Krist

docs.snippet: A family tragedy has left this novel’s twin narrators unrecognizable to themselves and each other.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I’ll Give You the Sun,” the second novel by the talented Jandy Nelson, author of “The Sky Is Everywhere,” is told from the alternating perspectives of teenage fraternal twins, a boy and girl named Noah and Jude, each of them narrating from a different side of the accident that forever changed their lives. On one level, the book is about duality: As Jude and Noah wrangle over who will go to a prestigious art school and vie for attention and approbation and even, for a short time, the affections of the same boy, each narrator struggles to become whole, to become something other than merely half of one. Although Nelson portrays the relationship between the twins, their oneness, as comforting, more often it is claustrophobic — perhaps contributing to the book’s tense, almost breathless feel. One of their favorite games is to divide up the world between them, choosing and bartering the sun or the trees or the oceans. There is the sense that the world is simply not big enough for both of them.

headline.main: ‘I’ll Give You the Sun,’ by Jandy Nelson
headline.print_headline: The Other Half of the Story

docs.abstract: A girl develops special powers after she survives a plague in this young adult novel.
docs.snippet: A girl develops special powers after she survives a plague in this young adult novel.
docs.lead_paragraph: It is “13 Juno, 1361,” and Adelina Amou­teru, a teenage girl from a place called Kenettra, is going to be burned at the stake for committing a murder. Several years earlier, we learn, a blood fever spread across this land. Most infected adults died. Children sometimes survived. Some of these children emerged without any sign of the infection; others, like Adelina, were marked and strangely scarred, their hair changing in color. These children, known as malfettos, are considered to have no social value and are persecuted by the government. Adelina’s own father, who regarded her as worthless, was preparing to sell her off to a business associate as a mistress to complete a deal. She decided to escape rather than accept this fate, and in the process accidentally killed her father. It is this act that has brought her to the stake, an uncompromising opening to “The Young Elites,” Marie Lu’s first novel after her hugely popular ­Legend series.

docs.lead_paragraph: The story of Abraham Lincoln’s childhood, “The Better Angels,” is also a Christ story in a strange key. It opens with black-and-white images of the Lincoln Memorial, some suggestive of the view of an awe-struck visitor. The absence of color holds your eye (black-and-white has become a palette for gimmicks and obscure auteurs), as do several arcs traced by the camera, as if that visitor were looking up and even searching. The camera movements seem familiar not only because they mirror the physical effort of what it’s like to tilt your head and stretch your neck, to gape up at a cathedral window or gathering clouds, but also because they evoke Terrence Malick.

headline.main: Lincoln, the Beardless, Ethereal Youth
headline.print_headline: Lincoln, the Beardless, Ethereal Youth

docs.snippet: “Mario Botta: Architecture and Memory” focuses on Botta’s public projects, including the iconic San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and the Church of San Giovanni Battista in his home country of Switzerland.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Swiss architect Mario Botta once described his hometown as “madre e matrigna” — “mother and stepmother” — an apt description for the Italian-speaking Swiss province of Ticino, which possesses cultural sensibilities of both nations. And just like his nuanced patrimony, the architectural style Botta has honed over a 50-year career stems from a mixture of influences. His half-century of work is celebrated in “Mario Botta: Architecture and Memory,” a monograph just released from Silvana Editoriale ($60 at artbook.com).

docs.lead_paragraph: Purveying a strangely sweet vulgarity, the romantic comedy “Sex Ed” commiserates with Eddie (Haley Joel Osment), 23, a would-be geometry teacher who’s as much a virgin in the bedroom as in the classroom. docs.lead_paragraph: President Vladimir V. Putin has revised his opinion of an important piece of Soviet history, calling the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop pact that Moscow signed with Nazi Germany to divide up Eastern Europe not so bad. “The Soviet Union signed a nonaggression treaty with Germany,” Mr. Putin said during a meeting with historians on Wednesday, according to a Russian transcript of the meeting that the Kremlin released Thursday. “People say: ‘Ach, that’s bad.’ But what’s bad about that if the Soviet Union didn’t want to fight? What’s bad about it?” While the Soviet Union is accused of dividing Poland, he said, Poland actually seized part of Czechoslovakia when Germany attacked that country. “Serious research should show that those were the methods of foreign policy then,” Mr. Putin said. Five years ago he had called the very same pact “immoral.” The statement is likely to increase security concerns in Eastern European states, which have been jittery about Russia’s intentions ever since it seized Crimea in March. Mr. Putin signed a law in May mandating five years imprisonment for anyone convicted of trying to rehabilitate Nazism.

headline.main: Russia: Putin Defends Soviet-Nazi Pact

docs.abstract: When a new father takes time off from work, his whole family can benefit. But maybe his career won’t.
docs.snippet: When a new father takes time off from work, his whole family can benefit. But maybe his career won’t.
docs.lead_paragraph: Five months after Todd Bedrick’s daughter was born, he took some time off from his job as an accountant. The company he works for, Ernst & Young, offered paid paternity leave, and he decided to take six weeks — the maximum amount — when his wife, Sarah, went back to teaching. He learned how to lull the fitful baby to sleep on his chest and then to sit very still for an hour to avoid waking her. He developed an elaborate system for freezing and thawing his wife’s pumped breast milk. And each day at lunchtime, he drove his daughter to the elementary school where Sarah teaches so she could nurse. When she came home at the end of the day, he handed over the baby and collapsed on the couch.

headline.main: Paternity Leave: The Rewards and the Remaining Stigma

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: German troops were ambushed by an armored train in 1914.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: German troops were ambushed by an armored train in 1914.
docs.lead_paragraph: NORTHERN FRANCE — Exasperated by the defeat of their fresh army corps, the Germans this week resorted to a purposeless plan of laying Ypres in ruins and ashes. From guns concealed by a haystack they inflicted enormous damage on the town, but late in the afternoon the Germans met with summary punishment in a way for which they were completely unprepared. The puffing of a steam-engine warned them as they thought of the approach of a troop train. They waited their opportunity, expecting it to pass a section of the railway which was visible to them nearly two miles away. Their opportunity never came. They simply heard the terrific crash of the heavy guns, and within a few seconds they and their guns ceased to exist. The enemy had been surprised by an armored train — the first which the British had sent to the firing line. The armored train has now supported our artillery for several days. Its casualties up to date consist of one man wounded. — The New York Herald, European Edition, Nov. 8, 1914

headline.main: 1914: Armored Train Surprise

docs.lead_paragraph: Ever since my parents split up when I was 27, I fantasized about walking back into my childhood home, which they moved out of six years before they parted ways. The divorce seemed to invalidate my entire childhood. All the carefully saved bits and pieces that documented my existence before my 20s — concert T-shirts decorated with safety pins, a white jean skirt bought with babysitting money — were gone without explanation, tossed out by movers, lost in the chaos of a hasty real estate transaction or appropriated by new people passing through my parents’ now-separate lives.

docs.lead_paragraph: One evening last fall, Teddy Thompson stepped onto the stage at the Purple Crayon, a cultural center in Hastings-on-Hudson, not far from New York City. The venue regularly attracts established pop-folk singers, the kind embraced by the public-radio-listening, Subaru-driving locals; Thompson loosely falls into that category, although he has the louche glamour of a heartbreaker, as well as the reputation (“I haven’t been invited on the Lilith tour,” he once dryly pointed out in an interview). Tall, fair, lean and British, he sang that night, with what one admiring critic has called his “keening tenor,” a series of songs about failed relationships in which Thompson, single at 38, was usually the bad actor: “I was born with a love disease/It’s known as chronic hard-to-please.”

headline.main: Teddy Thompson’s Folk-Rock Family Reunion

docs.lead_paragraph: A few minutes before 8 o’clock one Sunday evening last July, around 600 people crowded into the main conference hall of the South Point casino in Las Vegas. After taking their seats on red-velvet upholstered chairs, they chattered noisily as they awaited the start of the Million Dollar Challenge. When Fei Wang, a 32-year-old Chinese salesman, stepped onto the stage, they fell silent. Wang had a shaved head and steel-framed glasses. He wore a polo shirt, denim shorts and socks. He claimed to have a peculiar talent: from his right hand, he could transmit a mysterious force a distance of three feet, unhindered by wood, metal, plastic or cardboard. The energy, he said, could be felt by others as heat, pressure, magnetism or simply “an indescribable change.” Tonight, if he could demonstrate the existence of his ability under scientific test conditions, he stood to win $1 million.

docs.abstract: A recreation of William Blake’s London studio will be the centerpiece of an exhibition at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.
docs.snippet: A recreation of William Blake’s London studio will be the centerpiece of an exhibition at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — A recreation of William Blake’s London studio, based on a discovery of the original building plans, will be the centerpiece of the exhibition “Apprentice & Master” at the Ashmolean Museum of the University of Oxford, the museum announced Friday. The studio will be reconstructed to the exact dimensions detailed in the plans of No.13 Hercules Building, Hercules Road in the suburb of Lambeth, where Blake lived and worked from 1791 to 1800, creating most of his illuminated books and developing his own method of color printing. It will show the artist’s workbench and printing equipment, including a marble slab, inking stone, boards, papers and a star-wheel rolling press as well as three original prints representing his work and interests at the time.

headline.main: Exhibition Will Feature Recreation of William Blake’s Studio

docs.lead_paragraph: In the title story of Diane Cook’s debut collection, three men, childhood friends, are stranded in a great lake on a lifeboat. They’re in the middle of a shipping route, and yet no one has passed them, no rescue is in sight. “I want you to write me a world in which that happens,” one of the friends asks the television writer on the boat. It’s a grim scene. They’re running out of food, they can’t sleep or stretch out, and old tensions between the men have started to renew. The television writer creates an origin story for their predicament: a “coup d’état” in Canada, hostages, armed gunmen. He names the imaginary show “Man v. Nature.” “Everything is man versus this and man versus that,” he says. “It’s so simple. . . . It’s man versus everything. It’s me. It’s you. It’s us. It’s in us.”

docs.abstract: Jill Lepore, whose “Secret History of Wonder Woman” is No. 12 on the hardcover nonfiction list, says “Wonder Woman’s origin story borrows from all the conventions of feminist utopian fiction.”
docs.snippet: Jill Lepore, whose “Secret History of Wonder Woman” is No. 12 on the hardcover nonfiction list, says “Wonder Woman’s origin story borrows from all the conventions of feminist utopian fiction.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Missing Link: The high-low appeal of cultural studies, in which academics devote serious attention to the meanings and implications of pop phenomena, is nothing new. But it may have reached its happy apotheosis with “The Secret History of Wonder Woman,” new at No. 12 on the hardcover nonfiction list, by the Harvard historian and New Yorker staff writer Jill Lepore. “It struck me that Wonder Woman’s origin story borrows from all the conventions of feminist utopian fiction,” Lepore said in a recent interview with Comic Book Resource (“the premier online comics magazine”). “I had never noticed that tie before, and I don’t think comics fans or comics historians necessarily noticed it, either — mainly because there’s not a great deal of overlap between comics historians and readers of feminist utopian fiction.” Among other things, Lepore’s book traces the pervasive bondage scenes in “Wonder Woman” to suffragist politics, and locates the comic at an important point on the timeline of feminism. “People often think of the women’s rights movement as having taken place in waves,” she told Comic Book Resource. “There’s a first wave that ends with the passage of the 19th Amendment in 1920, and a second wave that begins in the ’60s, and in between those two waves, it’s as if there’s nothing going on. But once you lift the veil on the secret history of Wonder Woman, right there in the middle in the 1940s, there’s Wonder Woman, inspired by the feminism of the first half of the century, and an inspiration for the feminism in the second half.”

docs.snippet: Edward Hirsch’s book-length elegy on the death of his 22-year-old son.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the summer of 2011, when Edward Hirsch’s 22-year-old son, Gabriel, died of cardiac arrest after taking a club drug at a party in Jersey City, I was writing about my 1-year-old son, Ronan, who would eventually die of Tay-Sachs disease before his third birthday. During the course of Ronan’s life, I wrote constantly, often through the night, gripped by a need to understand a world in which such suffering was possible; and also to try to mitigate my helplessness and despair by giving myself something to do. “Gabriel: A Poem” — part tribute; part existential howl; part intellectual investigation of our most primal emotions; part novella-like, buoyant, unsentimental romp through the life of Hirsch’s “wild spirit beloved son” — is the kind of wrenching, meticulous study of grief I craved at that time.

headline.main: ‘Gabriel,’ by Edward Hirsch

But the story she tells — now in greater detail in her inspiring Y.A. memoir, “Taking Flight” — is one of almost unimaginable turmoil and out-of-the-blue good fortune, much like the fairy-tale dances she now performs.

docs.lead_paragraph: In his previous book, “The Shallows” — essential reading about our Internet Age — Nicholas Carr, former executive editor of the Harvard Business Review and author of several books about technology, discussed the detrimental effects the Web has on our reading, thinking and capacity for reflection. In this new book, “The Glass Cage: Automation and Us,” similarly essential if slightly repetitive, Carr explains how certain aspects of automative technology can separate us from, well, Reality. How, for all its ­miraculous-seeming benefits, automation also can and often does impair our mental and physical skills, cause dreadful mistakes and accidents, particularly in medicine and aviation, and threaten to turn the algorithms we create as servants into our mindless masters — what sci-fi movies have been warning us about for at least two or three decades now. (As Carr puts it near the end of “The Glass Cage,” when “we become dependent on our technological slaves . . . we turn into slaves ourselves.”)

docs.lead_paragraph: Children, like nations, need heroes to call their own. Parson Mason Weems’s “Life of Washington” rolled off the presses in Philadelphia in 1800, mere months after the death of the father of our country, with Weems’s stated goal to inspire young Americans to emulate the great man’s shining example. We have that book to thank for the compelling image of the rambunctious 6-year-old George chopping down his father’s best cherry tree, then fessing up to his misdeed with the immortal words: “I cannot tell a lie.” The irrepressible parson, we now know, invented the scene out of whole cloth, which is certainly a tad ironic. Yet less cavalier authors than Weems have wrestled with the question of whether, or to what extent in the seemingly special case of a biography for young readers, a touch-up job might be in order. The 1940 Caldecott Medal winner, “Abraham Lincoln,” by Ingri and Edgar Parin d’Aulaire, ends with an illustration of the weary president resting contentedly in a favorite rocker, the Civil War having just come to a successful conclusion. You would never guess Lincoln had those theater tickets.

docs.abstract: Robert Darnton probes the history of censorship and finds it isn’t always what we think it is.
docs.snippet: Robert Darnton probes the history of censorship and finds it isn’t always what we think it is.
docs.lead_paragraph: The impulse to censor is as old as the impulse to create. Plato, not the most liberal of men, suggested that the work of storytellers should be carefully examined “and what they do well we must pass and what not, reject.” His purpose was to moralize literature; others, over the centuries, have offered equally noble motives. Ibn Khaldun, the great Arab historian, reported that in the seventh century, when Muslim soldiers invaded Persia, they discovered an extraordinary number of books; wishing to carry them off as loot, they asked Omar bin al-Khattab, second caliph of the Muslims, for permission. Omar’s answer became legendary and was applied to other book destructions: “Throw them in the river! If they hold a guide to the Truth, God has given us a better guide in the Holy Quran. And if they hold nothing but lies, may God rid us of them.” In our own time, the president of Turkey, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, forced Google and Twitter to remove content objected to by his government or risk blackouts, arguing that “these regulations do not impose any censorship at all on the Internet. . . . On the contrary, they make it safer and freer.” Morality, truth, civilized society, freedom: All these have been invoked to defend what most people would understand as censorship.

headline.main: ‘Censors at Work,’ by Robert Darnton
headline.print_headline: Watch Your Language

In “Arcady’s Goal,” an immensely rewarding novel by Eugene Yelchin, the protagonist’s parents are devoured in much the way the parents are devoured in “James and the Giant Peach.” Only instead of a rhino, it’s Stalin. And instead of the boy being made to live in the house of his mean aunts, he’s sent to a home for the offspring of “enemies of the state.” At the risk of seeming to equate the evils of the 20th century with the fiction of Roald Dahl: If you were born, say, in the early 2000s, the fate of a boy like Arcady might seem just as strange and unreal as anything cooked up by a fabulist from the middle of the last century.

docs.abstract: Jane Smiley’s novel, the first in a planned trilogy, follows an Iowa family over three transformative decades in America.
docs.snippet: Jane Smiley’s novel, the first in a planned trilogy, follows an Iowa family over three transformative decades in America.
docs.lead_paragraph: Before Marilynne Robinson’s Iowa, there was Jane Smiley’s. While Robinson, already revered as the author of “Housekeeping,” was taking a long pause from publishing to teach at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, Smiley wrote “A Thousand Acres,” a story of an Iowa farm family in extremis that won the Pulitzer Prize. While Robinson was writing “Gilead,” her own Pulitzer winner, and two subsequent novels about Iowa church people and their descendants, Smiley was shaking off the Heartland-Author tag with novels about real estate and tax evasion (“Good Faith”), Hollywood (“Ten Days in the Hills”) and a military wife transplanted from Missouri to San Francisco (“Private Life”). With a short biography of Dickens, she invited us to see her, like him, as a writer whose work is defined by its energy and range rather than its settings and subject matter. With a whistle-stop tour of 100 novels (“Thirteen Ways of Looking at the Novel”), she lined up with Henry James and John Updike as a writer who offsets her own fiction with spot-on commentary about other people’s work. So it’s appropriate to turn to “Some Luck” — the first novel in a projected trilogy about Iowa farm people and their descendants — by way of Smiley’s critical insights.

She was a regular second grader and she talked to trees. I don’t think she’s the only one. Trees have always played a central role in the lives and minds of our species. Researchers tell us that surgical patients heal faster when their windows look out on trees and children do better in school when they can see green spaces. When the famous Treaty Oak in Austin, Tex., was poisoned in 1989, kids made hundreds of cards and placed them under the tree. Not all kids live near historic oaks, but most care about trees, and wonder about them. Books about trees speak to that wondering.

docs.abstract: From Washington to Paris, four interwoven characters grapple with guilt and injustice.
docs.snippet: From Washington to Paris, four interwoven characters grapple with guilt and injustice.
docs.lead_paragraph: Incarcerated in the German prisoner-of-war camp Stalag VIII-A in 1940, the French composer Olivier Messiaen set down what he called “Quatuor Pour la Fin du Temps,” the “Quartet for the End of Time.” It was first performed in January 1941 before a freezing audience of prisoners and German guards. The reception was said to have been respectful if bemused. As the critic Alex Ross later explained: “By 1941, this composer no longer wanted to hear time being beaten out by a drum — one, two, three, four; he had had enough of that in the war. Instead, he devised rhythms that expanded, contracted, stopped in their tracks and rolled back in symmetrical patterns.” The quartet, Ross observed, is “the most ethereally beautiful music of the 20th century.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Like a bad haircut, the word “alien” has affixed itself to the popular perception of what it means to be Latino in the United States. To the unworldly, the average working person of Latin American descent looks like an “illegal alien.” For decades Latino comedians have been making satirical commentary on the absurdity (and cruelty) of using the same word to describe people with Spanish surnames and slimy creatures from other worlds, and now William Alexander has given us a middle-grade novel that stretches out the joke for an entire book. Alexander, who won a National Book Award for his 2012 novel “Goblin Secrets,” merges the fantastic with the ­everyday to create an engaging and smart allegory about the hurt and strangeness of the modern immigrant condition.

The authors are describing Schmidt’s first years as C.E.O., when the board of directors was consumed with worry about its most formidable competitor, Microsoft. Back then Google employees, the authors write, referred to their archrival by a secret code name: “Finland.” It seems like a fresh if somewhat inexplicable detail, until the eye wanders down to the bottom of the page and this disclaimer: “In fact, ‘Finland’ is a code name for the code name we actually used. If we used the actual code name in this book, it wouldn’t be much of a code name, would it?”

docs.lead_paragraph: Scott Westerfeld’s semi-supernatural novel “Afterworlds” beckons us into a universe where dutiful drones, pale from sun deprivation, spend long, lonely days toiling at an irksome task in order to prove their worth. The challenges they face are many, and their chances of survival, let alone success, are low. Though these worker bees occasionally bond with others of their ilk, they’re really on their own, forever outrunning the authority figures who regularly swoop down to assess their accomplishments and mete out punishment accordingly. The stakes are high: If the denizens of this universe fail, they’ll be dropped into the black hole of obscurity where, unless they can claw their way out, they’ll languish forever.

docs.abstract: Two young adult thrillers exploit the conventions of genre to offer head-on critiques of today’s political landscape.
docs.snippet: Two young adult thrillers exploit the conventions of genre to offer head-on critiques of today’s political landscape.
docs.lead_paragraph: To be a teenager is to be acutely aware of power, in all its forms — by virtue of having so frustratingly little of it. Which means adolescent protagonists impose a limiting factor on political fiction. Young adult authors looking to vent their political spleen commonly circumvent this with one of two routes: They embrace George Eliot’s reminder that “there is no private life which has not been determined by a wider public life,” filtering political exigencies through the lens of personal experience and mapping out the Machiavellian power plays of home and high school. Or they turn to science fiction and fantasy and play politics to their heart’s content: There’s no believability ceiling to how teenagers in futuristic societies can change their worlds.

docs.lead_paragraph: The singer and songwriter Nick Drake had scant success in his lifetime, despite enthusiastic reviews and a following among English folksingers in the late 1960s and early 1970s. After three albums that sold only modestly, he was dropped by his label, and he died in 1974, at 26, of an overdose of antidepressant drugs. Since his death, however, Drake’s music has won a large and still growing following, not least among young listeners tuned to the emotional fragility of his songs, and attracted by the romantic image of a darkly mysterious, sensitive songwriter who died too young.

docs.snippet: The artist’s newest work, partially inspired by Willem de Kooning, emphasizes complex layering techniques that obscure the paintings’ subjects.
docs.lead_paragraph: Last June, the Metropolitan Museum of Art asked the artist George Condo to participate in a discussion on Willem de Kooning. In the course of his research on de Kooning, Condo read several texts by the art critic Harold Rosenberg and became inspired by the concept of “action painting” — the term Rosenberg coined to describe the intense, almost performative energy the Abstract Expressionists used to paint their canvases. Condo experimented with that idea while creating his newest body of work earlier this year in his East Hampton studio. “They coalesced into the form of a portrait, rather than just a sort of abstract painting,” Condo says. That series, which he calls “action portraits,” is on view from Nov. 8 to Dec. 20, in a 12-piece exhibition titled “Double Heads / Black Paintings / Abstractions” at Skarstedt’s Chelsea location.

headline.main: George Condo Creates Portraits in Action

Oldest story in the book: A developer is tearing down the building and putting up — what else? — condominiums. To celebrate (or rather, mourn) the end of his temple to molecular gastronomy, Mr. Dufresne has devised a pair of menus for his last few weeks, and on Wednesday night they drew a crowd of curious first timers, former employees back for a last repast and a man who is widely acknowledged as the restaurant’s best customer: Stewart Waltzer, an art dealer who has dined at WD-50 more than 300 times and has booked a table for each remaining Wednesday of the month.

(Showtime) AUGUST: OSAGE COUNTY A dysfunctional clan unfurls its secrets as it gathers to mourn the loss of its patriarch in this dark comedy, directed by John Wells and adapted by Tracy Letts from his Pulitzer Prize-winning play. Sam Shepard portrays Beverly Weston, an alcoholic poet living in a rambling farmhouse in northeastern Oklahoma who hires a Native American caretaker (Misty Upham) for his shrill, pill-addicted wife, Violet (Meryl Streep) — and then disappears. Julia Roberts, Ms. Nicholson and Ms. Lewis and play Beverly and Violet’s daughters; Ewan McGregor, Dermot Mulroney and Benedict Cumberbatch are the men in their lives. And Margo Martindale and Chris Cooper are Violet’s sister and brother-in-law, who are there to lend support. But the story of the Weston family “is secondary to the spectacle the actors make of themselves,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times, calling the film “a thespian cage match” in which “a bunch of unquestionably talented performers is assembled with no instructions other than to top one another.” He added, “It goes without saying that nobody can beat Ms. Streep at this game.” (She received an Oscar nomination, as did Ms. Roberts.) “But everyone joins in.”

docs.lead_paragraph: The comedian Tig Notaro canceled shows in Boston and Denver over the weekend because of an unspecified “medical emergency,” according to promoters of the performances. Notes on the Facebook accounts of the Wilbur Theater in Boston, where Ms. Notaro was scheduled to perform on Saturday, and AEG Live Rocky Mountains, which promoted Sunday’s event in Denver, said that tickets would be refunded and the shows rescheduled. “Tig is dealing with a medical emergency and is being hospitalized,” a post on the AEG Live Rocky Mountain account said. “She will be all right but has to cancel the show tonight.” Calls and emails to Ms. Notaro’s manager were not returned on Sunday. Ms. Notaro has publicly battled breast cancer, working her diagnosis into her 2012 comedy routine; she received a 2013 Grammy nomination for her comedy album “Live.” She performed at the New York Comedy Festival on Thursday, and received critical praise for her act. Ms. Notaro performed most of the show topless, revealing scars from a double mastectomy with no reconstruction. The next stop on her “Boyish Girl Interrupted” tour is Portland, Ore. As of Sunday afternoon, that sold-out performance was still scheduled for Wednesday night.

headline.main: Tig Notaro Faces ‘Medical Emergency’

docs.lead_paragraph: The theater company Primary Stages announced on Sunday that it would move forward with its Off Broadway Oral History Project, which seeks to create a video archive of interviews with the actors, directors, designers, producers, playwrights and theater founders who have participated in Off and Off Off Broadway since World War II. The project is the brainchild of Casey Childs, the Primary Stages founder, who said he considered the idea for years after noticing a lack of firsthand information about this part of the theater world. Since July, Mr. Childs, the director Sally Plass and a team of interns have recorded about 50 hours of interviews with 20 Off Broadway leaders, including the actors Fyvush Finkel and Arthur French, the Chelsea Theater Center founder Robert Kalfin, the Playwrights Horizons founder Robert Moss and the Pan Asian Repertory Theater founder Tisa Chang. Mr. Childs said the goal was to record at least 100 interviews to be made available to the public online in the next six to 12 months. “It’s important to do because these people are dying every day,” Mr. Childs said in a phone interview. “It’s a race against the clock, but we’re getting them.” He said that he was in talks with several universities and foundations to host the videos but that it was too early to name the candidates.

headline.main: Oral History Project at Primary Stages

docs.snippet: How many honey pots could a silly old bear fill if he had 100,000 British pounds, or roughly $159,000?
docs.lead_paragraph: How many honey pots could a silly old bear fill if he had 100,000 British pounds, or roughly $159,000? That’s the low estimate for an original illustration from A. A. Milne’s 1928 book “The House at Pooh Corner” to be sold at Sotheby’s London next month. The drawing, signed by the artist E. H. Shepard, depicts Winnie-the-Pooh playing a game of “Poohsticks” on a bridge with Christopher Robin and Piglet. It has been part of a private collection since 1975, according to the Sotheby’s London sale catalog. The illustration is expected to fetch £100,000 to £150,000, or about $159,000 to $238,000, and is one of several drawings by Shepard that the auction house will feature at its “English Literature, History, Children’s Books and Illustration” sale on Dec. 9. Other items include drawings by Beatrix Potter and Edmund Dulac, a copy of “Peter Pan” signed by J. M. Barrie, and presentation copies of uncorrected “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets” proofs signed by J. K. Rowling. Pooh has proved to be a lucrative draw at previous auctions. In November 2008, an original Shepard sketch of Pooh and friends sold for about $50,100 at a Bonham’s auction. A month later, the Stanley J. Seeger and Christopher Cone collection of Shepard’s original drawings for the Winnie-the-Pooh books brought in about $1.97 million at a Sotheby’s London auction.

headline.main: Pooh Illustrations to Be Auctioned

docs.abstract: To gain an advantage when hunting, Mexican free-tailed bats emit a special call that interferes with the calls of other bats in search of food, researchers say.
docs.snippet: To gain an advantage when hunting, Mexican free-tailed bats emit a special call that interferes with the calls of other bats in search of food, researchers say.
docs.lead_paragraph: To gain an advantage when hunting, Mexican free-tailed bats emit a special call that interferes with the calls of other bats in search of food, researchers say. Bats navigate by making calls and sensing where the sound echoes off objects. But researchers from Wake Forest University who studied recordings of hunting bats in two outdoor sites found that bats can jam competitors’ frequencies by producing a special signal, making it difficult for them to locate their prey’s position. Writing in the journal Science, the researchers noted that the bats being targeted by a jamming signal can emit their own special signal in retaliation.

headline.main: A Bat Signal Is Jammed

docs.lead_paragraph: The week of back-to-back important postwar and contemporary art auctions kicks off at Sotheby’s on Monday night with masterworks from the estate of Rachel Lambert Mellon, known as Bunny. docs.lead_paragraph: Not long after they first emerged in the underground music scene in mid-1960s London, Pink Floyd earned a reputation, as Rolling Stone put it in 2007, as the city’s “farthest-out group.” And as art students at the time they got together, the band members — the bassist Roger Waters, the singer Syd Barrett, the drummer Nick Mason and the pianist Rick Wright; Barrett was later replaced by David Gilmour — firmly believed their aesthetic was as important as the notes they played. The Floyd, as they were known, provided audiences with a complete sensory experience, pairing visceral, operatic lyrics with elaborate light projections that seemed to move in turn to the music. And even as they achieved global popularity in the 1970s with a string of landmark albums including 1973’s “The Dark Side of the Moon,” 1975’s “Wish You Were Here” and 1979’s “The Wall,” the band remained focused on bringing visual ideas to the forefront through their live shows and iconic album art.

headline.main: Artists on How Pink Floyd Influenced Them

docs.abstract: Why the Union destroyed the Georgia city, through the eyes of one Union officer.
docs.snippet: Why the Union destroyed the Georgia city, through the eyes of one Union officer.
docs.lead_paragraph: On the evening of Nov. 15, 1864, Union Lt. Col. Charles Fessenden Morse sat on the roof of a house and watched Atlanta burn. It was a “magnificent and awful spectacle,” he wrote later to his brother Robert. “For miles around the country was as light as day, … the flames shooting up for hundreds of feet into the air.” Earlier, over the roar and crackle of the flames, Morse had heard the 33rd Massachusetts band serenade Gen. William Tecumseh Sherman, who ordered the city torched. “It was like fiddling over the burning of Rome.” The next morning, nothing was left of the city “except its churches the city hall and the private dwellings. You could hardly find a vestige of the once splendid R.R. depots, warehouses, &c. It was melancholy,” Morse lamented, “but it was war, prosecuted in deadly earnest.”

headline.main: The Burning of Atlanta

docs.lead_paragraph: Federal regulators on Monday restricted commercial fishing for Atlantic cod in the Gulf of Maine. Officials with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced a temporary emergency action that establishes rolling restrictions to commercial boats with gear capable of catching cod in areas of the gulf. It also limited catches to 200 pounds per trip in areas that remain open. Earlier this year, the administration released a study showing stocks of the species to be at historically low levels. The action will be in effect through the spring, but similar terms could be extended for the 2015 fishing season. Some fishermen said the cuts could put them out of business. Also Monday, the regulators increased the amount of haddock that fishermen are allowed to catch.

docs.lead_paragraph: American Apparel, a beleaguered retailer still wincing from a boardroom struggle over the summer, said sales fell 5 percent in the third quarter and losses grew — dragged down in no small part by its own investigation of the behavior of Dov Charney, who was fired as chief executive in June. The company, which has been without a permanent chief executive ever since, reported a net loss of $19.2 million, or 11 cents a share, most of which was nonrecurring costs, including $5.3 million in legal and other costs connected to Mr. Charney’s departure. A year ago, the net loss was $1.5 million. Net sales in the third quarter slipped to $155.9 million, compared with $164.5 million last year. Highlighting the company’s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, which jumped 38 percent to $13.5 million, Scott Brubaker, the interim chief, said in a statement, “I am encouraged by these results, and am optimistic about the future prospects of the business.”

docs.lead_paragraph: “Heaven,” the debut EP from T.O.L.D., runs a bit like a three-act play. It opens with “Lucifer’s Eyes,” a deceptively upbeat electro-pop tune that lays bright steel-drum sounds over pulsing synth lines and warm, dreamy backing vocals — elements that carry into “In Low Light,” which leads with a guitar intro that wouldn’t be out of place in a song by the XX. Like that band’s music, and others to which the project will draw comparison (Tanlines or Discovery, perhaps), the EP, which will be released Nov. 18 and premieres here, finds unexpected balances between lightness and darkness. “You focus on the beauty, but you use the sadness as a skeleton,” says Dan Smith, the 24-year-old Birmingham-born artist behind the project.

To mark the organization’s 20th anniversary this month, however, its director Joe Scotland is teaming up with a much more recognizable name. Beginning tomorrow and running through December, the studio will open the third installation of its biennial pop-up shop, taking place this year in partnership with Chloé and its creative director Clare Waight Keller. The temporary store, House of Voltaire, which opens tomorrow in Mayfair, will sell a curated selection of commissioned home décor, limited edition prints and artworks as well as clothing and accessories by a variety of artists and designers. Chloé has also created a special four-piece capsule collection — a bag by Waight Keller, a top and shorts by the painter Karen Kilimnik, a dress by the multimedia artist Cao Fei and a scarf by the painter Jenny Saville — all of which will also be available on Net-a-Porter starting Friday, Nov. 14.

docs.lead_paragraph: When you pull off Highway 101 and head into Sunnyvale, Calif., the first thing you notice is how boring innovation looks up close. This small Silicon Valley city, which abuts both Cupertino, the home of Apple, and Mountain View, the site of the Googleplex, is where Lockheed built the Poseidon nuclear missile. It’s where the forebear of NASA did some of its most important research and where a prototype for Pong debuted at a neighborhood bar. Countless ambitious start-ups — with names like Qvivr, Schoolfy, eCloset.me and PeerPal — appear in Sunnyvale every year. Aesthetically, though, the city is one enormous glass-and-stucco office park after another. Its dominant architectural feature, the five-story headquarters of Yahoo, a few minutes from Innovation Way, looks about as futuristic as a suburban hospital.

docs.abstract: Two new books show how photography can bring a picture book to life.
docs.snippet: Two new books show how photography can bring a picture book to life.
docs.lead_paragraph: The picture-book version of the French film “The Red Balloon” was a treasured possession of my 1970s childhood. I was enthralled not just by the story of the lonely boy and his mysterious balloon companion but also — and perhaps even more — by the photography. Each page of the book is a still from the movie, a thrillingly lucid, beautifully stylized window into the real world. The photos were of Paris, not fancy Paris but the gray, gray Paris of crumbling buildings and dim alleyways. The camera made each pockmarked wall look like an elaborate Modernist painting, with the little boy dressed in soft dove-gray himself a lovely detail in it — and then set against all the grayness on each page was that miraculous balloon. It glided across the scene, redder than any red and bigger than any balloon I’d ever seen, a beacon of pure joy and a testament to the possibility that a bit of magic could float right into your tough everyday life.

docs.lead_paragraph: Taylor Swift’s “1989” remains at the top of the Billboard 200 for a second week, not surprisingly, with sales of 402,000 copies during the week ending Nov. 9, the magazine and Nielsen SoundScan reported. That is a drop of 69 percent from Ms. Swift’s first-week sales, but it means that in the two weeks since the album was released, it has sold nearly 1.7 million copies, an extraordinary number these days. By contrast, the disc holding the No. 2 sales spot – the 52nd installment of the “Now That’s What I Call Music!” – sold 59,000 in its second week on the chart, after 103,000 last week, for combined sales that are less than a tenth of Ms. Swift’s.

docs.lead_paragraph: Ron Arad, the Israeli-born, London-based designer, doesn’t appreciate a fussy table setting and is anything but a wine snob. Speaking at a press conference in Istanbul earlier this year, he said that the subtleties of wineglass varieties eluded him; a vintage registers on his palate as good or bad, no matter the size or shape of its container. Having been asked to create glassware for the Turkish manufacturer Pasabahce, he accepted that different vessels were necessary for red and white wine, but saw no reason that they couldn’t be conjoined. That is how he came up with the Red/White goblet, into which you can pour either color simply by which way you turn the glass. The goblet is one of eight pieces Mr. Arad designed for the Pasabahce glassware collection called Nude (the name refers to the objects’ transparency). It will be available in spring and cost $150 for a pair. Information: 212-683-1600.
