docs.lead_paragraph: South Asian leaders discussed trade and energy cooperation and regional peace in Katmandu on Wednesday, but did not reach a consensus on expected transportation and energy agreements. Hopes for a meeting between the leaders of India and Pakistan also appeared to fade. In opening remarks Wednesday at the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation summit meeting, the first since 2011, Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India noted that it was the anniversary of the 2008 attacks on Mumbai, in which Pakistani gunmen killed 166 people. Relations between India and Pakistan were frozen after the attacks, and little progress has been made since. The signing of deals on the sharing of railroads, highways and energy had been expected, but unless one is achieved during a retreat on Thursday, the meeting could end without any agreements signed.

The announcement did not provide details of the charges against the leader, María Corina Machado, but this year senior government officials accused her of organizing a conspiracy to kill the president. They showed what they claimed were a series of emails that they said implicated Ms. Machado and other opposition figures. They also said that Kevin Whitaker, a former State Department official who is now ambassador to Colombia, was implicated in the scheme. Ms. Machado is a former legislator and an ally of another politician, Leopoldo López, who was jailed this year after weeks of protests against the government. Mr. Maduro, a leftist who faces a severe economic crisis, has frequently said his enemies are plotting to kill or overthrow him.

docs.lead_paragraph: The smoking rate in the United States declined to 17.8 percent in 2013, down slightly from 18.1 percent the previous year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported Wednesday. The report found a decline in the number of smokers in the United States — 42 million in 2013, down from 45 million in 2005 — despite an increase in population. The smoking rate has been dropping for decades, but the pace of the decline has slowed in recent years. The smoking rate was 20.9 percent in 2005 and stood at about 42 percent in 1965, when the federal government began systematically tracking it.

docs.lead_paragraph: “The Imitation Game” is a highly conventional movie about a profoundly unusual man. This is not entirely a bad thing. Alan Turing’s tragically shortened life — he was 41 when he died in 1954 — is a complex and fascinating story, bristling with ideas and present-day implications, and it benefits from the streamlined structure and accessible presentation of modern prestige cinema. The science is not too difficult, the emotions are clear and emphatic, and the truth of history is respected just enough to make room for tidy and engrossing drama.

docs.snippet: “The Babadook,” the Australian director Jennifer Kent’s debut feature, is a horror movie full of interlocking ambiguities.
docs.lead_paragraph: I was an easily frightened child, and nothing scared me more than certain picture books. Something about the static images, the simple words and the unseen menaces hidden between pages made books much more sinister than, say, movies, and quite a few volumes that now seem perfectly innocuous were banished from my bedroom shelves. I had forgotten about this youthful phobia until I saw “The Babadook,” the debut feature by the Australian director Jennifer Kent. Or rather, until I came home from the screening, went to bed and woke up in the throes of the kind of nightmare that was the reason I had shunned those books in the first place.

docs.lead_paragraph: At a time when news about Africa has been dominated by Ebola, it’s worth observing that a highly encouraging change has been quietly spreading across the continent. Over the past five years, the number of Africans — mainly women — who have joined village-based savings and loan associations has soared to more than nine million. These groups are now operating in 40 countries in Africa. Globally, it’s estimated that 10.5 million people are members of formally trained savings groups in about 65 countries. docs.lead_paragraph: One day in 1980, I reached a milestone in a Jewish boy’s journey into manhood: spending my bar mitzvah money on punk rock records. I was searching the racks at a record store for “Adult Books,” the debut single by the Los Angeles band X, and the only 45 that remotely fit the bill featured a couple of white X’s on the front cover, separated by a dash, above a photo of the bare backside of a woman bound at the ankles. The back-cover band photo corresponded somewhat to the group I’d read about in a zine — four members, one of them female — though the label credited the single to Drome Records instead of Dangerhouse. So a band name starting with “X,” a multigendered quartet, a record label beginning with “D,” a whiff of the forbidden: “Close enough,” I thought, and made my purchase.

docs.snippet: The photographs of Spot, a record producer and key figure of the era, are collected in a new volume, “The Sound of Two Eyes Opening.”
docs.lead_paragraph: In punk and hardcore circles, the name Spot is legend. Born in Southern California, Spot produced albums for some of the most seminal bands of those scenes in the ’70s and ’80s — Black Flag, the Misfits, the Minutemen, the Meat Puppets and Hüsker Du among them. When he wasn’t behind the mixing board at SST Records, the label founded by Black Flag’s Greg Ginn, he was likely to be roller-skating the boardwalks — or behind the lens of his Nikon, photographing the skate ramps, the beaches, the house parties. Bruised and bloodied and tanned from the day’s skating, everyone would head to see whichever band was playing that night, and then Spot would stay up late in the darkroom afterwards. Those sleepless, exciting times are documented in Spot’s first book of photographs, “The Sound of Two Eyes Opening,” out Friday from Sinecure.

docs.snippet: In “There Was a Little Girl,” No. 11 on the hardcover nonfiction list, Brooke Shields writes frankly and tenderly about her mother.
docs.lead_paragraph: Mother and Daughter: The cover of Brooke Shields’s latest memoir, “There Was a Little Girl” (new on the hardcover nonfiction list at No. 11), shows the author sometime in the mid-1970s, relaxing happily on the lap of her mother and manager, Teri Shields, their hands touching and their heads tilted girlishly together. It’s a sweet and wholesome image, and a far cry from a photo that ran around the same time on the cover of New York magazine, depicting Brooke in full makeup with a haughty stare while her mother grasped her shoulders. “Meet Teri and Brooke Shields,” the cover read. “Brooke is 12. She poses nude. Teri is her mother. She thinks it’s swell.” Shields doesn’t mention that article in her book, which is subtitled “The Real Story of My Mother and Me,” but she does talk about the media uproar surrounding Louis Malle’s 1978 film “Pretty Baby,” in which she played an underage prostitute, and all of the racy jobs that followed. “There was a sense of fury and a need to assume that I was a victim,” she writes. “There was a firestorm, and Mom took most of the heat.” Although Shields writes frankly and painfully about her mother’s chronic drinking and poor career decisions, the book — which was prompted, she says, by her reaction to The New York Times’s obituary after Teri Shields died in 2012 — is mostly tender. “It is not a ‘Mommie Dearest’ tale. But I’m not holding her up on a pedestal, either,” she writes. “It is simply my turn to tell the story as I saw and felt it.”

docs.lead_paragraph: The choreographer Neil Greenberg is allergic to the word “about” when it comes to discussing his dances. Aren’t the days of dances having to be about something long gone? Inspired by Susan Sontag’s “Against Interpretation,” Mr. Greenberg, in his new dance “This,” fights the idea that meaning must be assigned to choreography. His last work, “(like a vase),” presented four years ago, explored the tension created by the desire for meaning. In “This,” he goes further by focusing on dance as a crystallization of the performance moment.

I read some books on the subject, but most were tripper’s guides that didn’t utilize, um, specific language or current science. Psychoactive mushrooms had been in a kind of scientific ghetto ever since they were criminalized in 1968. docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The Metropolitan Opera House reopens in New York in 1889.
docs.lead_paragraph: Wealth, art and society were well represented at the reopening of the Metropolitan Opera House. It marked the beginning of the sixth season of opera in German. The house had a brilliant appearance when the curtain rose on the first act of Wagner’s “Flying Dutchman.” Although it rained in torrents all the evening, the ladies appeared in their rarest toilettes, and the boxes literally blazed with diamonds. Mrs. Astor was in white pink brocade, and occupied a box with Miss Marion Longdon and Mr. Ward McAlister. Miss Longdon wore pale yellow with a long boa of ostrich feathers. In an adjoining box sat Mrs. William C. Whitney in a décolleté dress of pale green and silver, with diamonds in her hair. Mrs. Paran Stevens wore a brocade toilette, and Mrs. Cornelius Vanderbilt wore white brocade and pearls. On the stage interest centred chiefly in Theodore Reichmann, the popular Viennese barytone, and in Fraulein Sophie Weisner, the soprano, who made their debut in this country as Senta and Vanderdecken. Reichmann scored a great and instant success, thanks as much to his admirable and artistic acting as to his rich and sympathetic voice. Fraulein Weisner’s success was less emphatic, although, like Reichmann, she was warmly applauded. — The New York Herald, European Edition, Dec. 1, 1889

headline.main: 1889: Metropolitan Opera House Reopens in New York

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Russians dominate in East Poland in 1914.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Russians dominate in East Poland in 1914.
docs.lead_paragraph: PETROGRAD — The steady increase in the strength of the Russian troops is transforming the appearance of the battles in East Poland. During the recent fighting in this region, and more particularly on Thursday, the Germans have sustained enormous loss. After a multitude of charges by the Russian cavalry, the state of the fields and roads rendered the use of automobiles absolutely impossible. The Russians have consequently garaged a large number of their machines at Lodz, whither they are also sending hundreds of transport and ammunition wagons captured from the enemy. The prolongation of the struggle in the neighborhood of Lodz is probably due to the feverish activity on the German strategic railways on the Silesian frontier. The enemy is bringing up troops with all possible speed, and it is estimated that 50,000 men, or nearly half the garrison of Breslau, were despatched north-west to Czenstochowa to join the newly-formed army in that region. Another great battle is to be expected somewhere between Lodz and Kalisz. — The New York Herald, European Edition, Dec. 1, 1914

headline.main: 1914: Russians Dominate in East Poland

docs.lead_paragraph: At the American Contract Bridge League’s fall championships in Providence, R.I., the first two national titles were won on Saturday evening. The Smith Life Master Women’s Pairs was captured by Bronia Jenkins of Vero Beach, Fla., and Bernace De Young of Miami. They led after each of the four sessions, finishing three-tenths of a board ahead of Victoria Gromova and Tatiana Ponomareva from Russia. The Russians, who were second after each session, won this event in 2012. Third were Ljudmila Kamenova of South Setauket, N.Y., and Linda Lewis of Las Vegas.

docs.abstract: Philip Henry Duclos plays the Nutcracker and Sterling Hyltin the Sugarplum Fairy in “George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker,” from New York City Ballet.
docs.snippet: Philip Henry Duclos plays the Nutcracker and Sterling Hyltin the Sugarplum Fairy in “George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker,” from New York City Ballet.
docs.lead_paragraph: When did “The Nutcracker” become more than just a ballet? With its intoxicating mix of the fantastical and the human, this venerated dance is a ritual that has stuck around for good reason: How many works of art are able to capture memory and the passing of time so profoundly on both sides of the stage? “The Nutcracker” has as much importance for the dancers who grow up performing it as it does for the audience members who grow up watching it. The charge in the air is real; somehow the dancers and the audience unite in the middle.

docs.abstract: The No. 1 movie in North America was again “The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1.” But moviegoing over the Thanksgiving holiday dropped 21 percent compared with the period a year ago.
docs.snippet: The No. 1 movie in North America was again “The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1.” But moviegoing over the Thanksgiving holiday dropped 21 percent compared with the period a year ago.
docs.lead_paragraph: Moviegoing over the Thanksgiving holiday dropped 21 percent compared with the period a year ago, as two new wide-release movies, “Penguins of Madagascar” and “Horrible Bosses 2,” became the latest studio efforts to underperform. The No. 1 movie in North America was again “The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1,” which took in an estimated $56.9 million from Friday to Sunday, according to Rentrak, a box-office tracking firm. Domestic ticket sales for “Mockingjay” now total a hefty $225.7 million but are nonetheless running roughly 24 percent behind the last “Hunger Games” film.

docs.abstract: Jay Moss, 91, has made sculptures in his spare time throughout his life, but an exhibition of his work now on display at Manhattan College is only his second-ever solo show.
docs.snippet: Jay Moss, 91, has made sculptures in his spare time throughout his life, but an exhibition of his work now on display at Manhattan College is only his second-ever solo show.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Palisades were a blazing blur of orange, red and yellow, but Jay Moss had no time to savor the autumnal Hudson River view. He grabbed a small plank of soft wood and went to his bedroom, hunched over a band saw and slowly carved the contours of a masklike face. Specks of sawdust floated in the sunlight, their slightly burned odor filling the air.
